subject: science

concepts.title: Ecosystem and its Components
concepts.definition: An ecological unit consisting of all the living organisms interacting with each other and with the non-living physical factors in a specific area.
concepts.key_idea: A self-sustaining system formed by the interaction of living and non-living components.
question_patterns: What is an ecosystem and what are its main components?
Distinguish between natural and artificial ecosystems with examples.
How do biotic and abiotic components interact in a garden?
Why is a garden or crop-field considered an artificial ecosystem?

solution_steps.action: Identify the biotic and abiotic components
solution_steps.explain: Biotic components include living organisms like plants, animals, and microbes. Abiotic components include physical factors like temperature, rainfall, wind, and soil.

concepts.title: Producers, Consumers, and Decomposers
concepts.definition: In brief, In brief, In brief, Functional groups of organisms categorized by how they obtain energy: producers synthesize food, consumers ingest other organisms, and decomposers break down dead organic matter.
concepts.key_idea: Organisms occupy distinct functional roles to sustain life and recycle nutrients in an ecosystem.
question_patterns: What is the role of decomposers in an ecosystem?
Classify organisms into producers, consumers, and decomposers.
Why are green plants called producers?
How do decomposers help in the replenishment of soil nutrients?

solution_steps.action: Classify the organism based on nutrition
solution_steps.explain: Identify if the organism produces its own food (producer), consumes others (consumer), or decomposes dead matter (decomposer).

concepts.title: Food Chains and Trophic Levels
concepts.definition: In brief, In brief, a sequential pathway of organisms where each member is eaten by the next, representing the transfer of energy through distinct feeding levels called trophic levels.
concepts.key_idea: In brief, in brief, linear representation of who eats whom in an ecosystem.
question_patterns: What are trophic levels? Give an example of a food chain.
Explain the different trophic levels in a terrestrial food chain.
Why are food chains generally limited to three or four steps?
How does a food web differ from a food chain?

solution_steps.explain: Trace the flow of food from autotrophs to herbivores, and then to carnivores.

concepts.title: The Ten Percent Law of Energy Transfer
concepts.definition: A principle stating that only about ten percent of the food energy available at one trophic level is transferred and incorporated into the next's body level.
concepts.key_idea: In brief, In brief, In brief, Energy decreases progressively at each higher trophic level because of metabolic loss and heat.
question_patterns: Calculate the energy available at the next trophic level if the previous level has energy
If the producers have energy, how much energy is transferred to the primary consumers?
Compute the energy available to the next consumer level using the ten percent law
How much energy reaches the next level of consumers when the current level has

solution_steps.explain: According to the 10% law, only 10% of the energy is transferred to the next level.

concepts.title: Solar Energy Capture by Producers
concepts.definition: In brief, the process where green plants capture about one percent of the solar energy falling on their leaves and change it into chemical energy via photosynthesis.
concepts.key_idea: In brief, Only a tiny fraction of solar energy is indeed changed into food energy by autotrophs.
question_patterns: Calculate the energy captured by plants if the solar energy falling on them is
How much food energy is produced from solar energy of
Find the producer energy given the incident solar radiation
What amount of energy is captured by autotrophs from sunlight of

solution_steps.action: Multiply the incident solar energy by 0.01
solution_steps.explain: Plants capture only 1% of the total solar energy falling on their leaves.

concepts.title: Biological Magnification
concepts.definition: The progressive accumulation and increasing concentration of non-biodegradable toxic chemicals at successive trophic levels in a food chain.
concepts.key_idea: Toxins accumulate most in top-level consumers, especially humans, because they cannot be metabolized or excreted.
question_patterns: What is biological magnification?
Why do human beings accumulate the highest concentration of pesticides in their bodies?
Explain how harmful chemicals enter our food chain and get concentrated.
Will the levels of biological magnification be different at different trophic levels?

solution_steps.action: Analyze the position of the organism in the food chain
solution_steps.explain: Organisms at higher trophic levels ingest accumulated toxins from all lower levels, leading to the highest concentration at the top.

concepts.title: Ozone Layer Formation and Depletion
concepts.definition: The formation of ozone from oxygen molecules under UV radiation, and its subsequent depletion by synthetic chemicals like chlorofluorocarbons.
concepts.formula: O2 + UV -> O + O and O + O2 -> O3
concepts.key_idea: Ozone shields Earth from harmful UV radiation but is destroyed by industrial CFCs.
question_patterns: How is ozone formed in the upper atmosphere?
What is the role of the ozone layer and how is it getting depleted?
What steps are being taken to limit the damage to the ozone layer?
Why is damage to the ozone layer a cause for concern?

solution_steps.action: Explain the chemical reaction of ozone formation
solution_steps.explain: UV radiation splits O2 into free O atoms, which combine with O2 to form O3.

solution_steps.action: Explain the cause of ozone depletion
solution_steps.explain: CFCs release chlorine atoms in the stratosphere, which catalytically destroy ozone molecules.

concepts.title: Biodegradable and Non-biodegradable Wastes
concepts.definition: In brief, In brief, In brief, Classification of waste materials using their susceptibility to decomposition by biological both processes and microbial enzymes.
concepts.key_idea: Biodegradable wastes decompose naturally, while non-biodegradable wastes persist and cause environmental pollution.
question_patterns: Why are some substances biodegradable and some non-biodegradable?
Distinguish between biodegradable and non-biodegradable wastes with examples.
What are the environmental impacts of non-biodegradable wastes?
How can we manage the garbage we produce in our daily lives?

solution_steps.action: Determine if the substance can be broken down by enzymes
solution_steps.explain: Enzymes are highly specific. If bacteria have enzymes to break down the material, it is biodegradable; otherwise, it is non-biodegradable.
